title: Ajanta's caves were carved in two widely separated eras
body: The earliest Buddhist caves at Ajanta in Maharashtra date to the second and first centuries BCE. A later period of work took place in the fifth and sixth centuries CE, when excavators added caves under Vakataka rule.
takeaway: The site preserves changing approaches to carving and painting across centuries of Buddhist patronage.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ajanta Caves
visual: carved cave entrances following the curve of a cliff above a wooded ravine

title: Eleven churches at Lalibela were cut from living rock
body: In the Ethiopian highlands, workers carved 11 churches into bedrock at Lalibela. UNESCO describes the medieval complex as a 13th-century New Jerusalem, with churches set below ground level and approached through excavated passages.
takeaway: The spaces between the churches took excavation too. Corridors and trenches are part of the design.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
visual: a cross-shaped stone church seen from above inside a deep square trench
